meaning: Attached to a Sino-Japanese noun to make a na-adjective. It means “-ic, -al, having the quality of ...” or “in terms of ...”.
connection: Sino-Japanese noun + 的 (〜的な + noun / 〜的に + verb / 〜的だ)

senses.label: -ic, -al
senses.meaning: Shows that something has a certain quality, tendency, or character, much like English “-ic” or “-al”. 「〜的」 as a whole is a na-adjective, so before a noun it becomes 「〜的な」.
senses.connection: Sino-Japanese noun + 的な + noun / 的だ (経済的な, 具体的な, 積極的だ)
examples: Please give a more concrete example.
This town has many historic buildings.
His attitude is very proactive.

senses.label: In terms of ...
senses.meaning: As an adverb, 「〜的に」 means “in terms of ..., ...-ly”. For example, 「経済的に苦しい」 is “financially struggling”. It sounds more general than saying 「経済が」 directly.
senses.connection: Sino-Japanese noun + 的に + verb / adjective (経済的に, 時間的に, 基本的に)
examples: Time-wise, it's impossible to finish today.
Basically, we're off on weekends.
We support families that are struggling financially.

senses.label: Casual: as for ...
senses.meaning: In young people's casual speech, 「〜的には」 can follow a person or an ordinary noun to mean “as for ..., for me”. It sounds loose and vague. Don't use it in formal situations.
senses.connection: Noun + 的には (私的には, 気分的には)
examples: Mood-wise, I already feel like taking the rest of today off.
Personally, I like this design better.

notes: 「〜的」 attaches only to Sino-Japanese words, not usually to native Japanese words or loanwords. ✕「春的」, ○「春らしい」.
Before a noun you usually use 「〜的な」, but some set phrases attach directly: 「国際的協力」, 「科学的根拠」.
The 「的」 in 「目的」, 「的確」 and 「的中」 means “target”. It is not this pattern.

daily.title: Sharing an opinion with friends
daily.description: When a friend asks what you think, use 「〜的には」 to soften your personal view.
daily.example: Personally, I thought that movie was a bit long.

daily.title: Explaining your situation
daily.description: Turning down an invitation because money or time is tight.
daily.example: Money's a little tight for me this month.

daily.title: Reading the news
daily.description: Words with 「〜的」 appear all the time in news and newspapers.
daily.example: The government is considering drastic measures.

work.title: Making a proposal in a meeting
work.description: Asking a colleague to be more specific in a meeting.
work.example: Please give us a concrete schedule by next week.

work.title: Writing an evaluation
work.description: Objectively assessing an employee or project in a report.
work.example: He is extremely proactive about his work.

etymology: 「的」 was originally a Chinese suffix. In the Meiji era, Japanese translators used it heavily to render English adjective suffixes like “-tic” (romantic → 浪漫的). One theory says the sound of “-tic” also played a part. 「〜的」 then became a very productive suffix for making adjectives from Sino-Japanese words, and it even spread back into modern Chinese.

similar.title: 〜っぽい
similar.explanation: 「〜っぽい」 is casual and means “-ish, sort of like” (「子供っぽい」). It can attach to native Japanese words. 「〜的」 is more formal, attaches only to Sino-Japanese nouns, and sounds objective.

similar.title: 〜らしい (typical)
similar.explanation: 「〜らしい」 means “having the typical qualities something should have” (「春らしい天気」, 「男らしい」). 「〜的」 only describes a quality or aspect, with no sense of “living up to the name”.

similar.title: 〜化
similar.explanation: Both are Sino-Japanese suffixes. 「〜的」 makes adjectives (a quality); 「〜化」 makes nouns and する-verbs (becoming a state). 「具体的な案」 is a concrete plan; 「案を具体化する」 is to make a plan concrete.

meaning: Attached to a noun to mean “becoming ..., -ization”. Common forms are 「〜化する」 and 「〜化が進む」.
connection: Sino-Japanese noun / loanword + 化 (〜化する / 〜化される / 〜化が進む)

senses.label: Becoming a state
senses.meaning: Shows that something develops or changes into a certain state, like English “-ization” or “-ification”. It is often used for social or economic trends, and often goes with 「進む」 or 「進める」.
senses.connection: Noun + 化する / 化が進む (高齢化, 少子化, 自動化, 国際化)
examples: In Japan, the population is getting older and the birthrate is falling.
Almost all the work in the factory has been automated.
We respond to the globalization of business.

senses.label: Turning into another form
senses.meaning: Shows turning something into a different form, such as making a novel into a film or putting documents into digital data. 「〜化する / 〜化される」 are common.
senses.connection: Noun + 化する (映画化, データ化, 文書化, 商品化)
examples: I hear this novel will be made into a movie next year.
We digitized all the paper documents.

notes: 「〜化」 usually attaches to Sino-Japanese words of two or more kanji, or to loanwords. 「文化」, 「変化」 and 「消化」 are fixed words, not this pattern.
As a verb it is the する-verb 「〜化する」. The passive 「〜化される」 is very common.
One-kanji words like 「悪化」, 「強化」 and 「激化」 are fixed vocabulary. Learn them as single words.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: News reports on social issues often use 「〜化」.
daily.example: Because of global warming, summers are getting hotter and hotter.

daily.title: Chatting about movies
daily.description: Talking about a favorite manga getting a film version.
daily.example: I hear that manga is getting a live-action version.

work.title: Suggesting improvements
work.description: Proposing a way to work more efficiently in a meeting.
work.example: If we systematize this task, we can cut the time in half.

work.title: Writing a report
work.description: Describing the results of an improvement in a report.
work.example: Thanks to streamlining our operations, overtime dropped sharply.

etymology: 「化」 originally means “change, transform” and comes from Chinese. In modern times, Japanese used it to translate English suffixes like “-ize / -ization” (modernize → 近代化), and it became a very productive word-forming suffix.

similar.title: 〜的
similar.explanation: 「〜的」 means “having the quality of” and makes adjectives; 「〜化」 means “becoming” and makes nouns or verbs. 「国際的な会社」 is an international company; 「会社の国際化」 is a company going international.

similar.title: 〜くなる・〜になる
similar.explanation: 「〜になる」 is the general “become” and works with anything. 「〜化」 is a formal Sino-Japanese suffix, attaches only to nouns, and usually describes broad social or technical trends.

similar.title: 〜つつある
similar.explanation: 「〜つつある」 shows a change in progress and often combines with 「〜化」: 「高齢化しつつある」. 「〜化」 by itself only says what something becomes, not that it is in progress.

meaning: Read 「ちゅう」, it means “in the middle of ..., during ...”. Read 「じゅう」, it means “all through ..., throughout ...”.
connection: Noun + 中 (ちゅう: 会議中・今週中 / じゅう: 一日中・世界中)

senses.label: In the middle of
senses.meaning: Read 「ちゅう」. Attached to an action noun, it shows that something is in progress: “in a meeting, under construction, open”. Very common on signs and in phone calls.
senses.connection: Action noun + 中 (会議中, 電話中, 工事中, 営業中, 使用中)
examples: The department manager is in a meeting right now.
This road is under construction and closed.
Please don't use your phone during class.

senses.label: Within a period
senses.meaning: Read 「ちゅう」. Attached to a time noun, it means “within that period”. 「〜中に」 often marks a deadline. 「今日中」 and 「今年中」 are also often read 「じゅう」.
senses.connection: Time noun + 中 (に) (午前中, 今週中, 休み中, 留守中)
examples: Please submit this document by the end of this week.
I'll be home in the morning.
A package arrived while I was out.

senses.label: All through, throughout
senses.meaning: Read 「じゅう」. With a time noun it means “the whole ...”; with a place noun it means “all over ...”.
senses.connection: Time / place noun + 中 (一日中, 一年中, 世界中, 日本中, 家中)
examples: It rained all day yesterday.
This song is sung all over the world.
I searched the whole house for my keys.

notes: Rule of thumb: “in progress / within a period” is 「ちゅう」; “the whole time / whole area” is 「じゅう」.
「今日中」 and 「今年中」 can be read either way; 「じゅう」 sounds more casual.
「途中」, 「最中」, 「背中」 and 「中国」 are fixed words, not this pattern.

daily.title: Answering the phone
daily.description: A family member tells the caller the person can't come to the phone.
daily.example: Sorry, my brother is taking a bath right now.

daily.title: Complaining about the weather
daily.description: Telling a friend it was hot all day.
daily.example: I had the air conditioner on all day today.

daily.title: Seeing a sign at a shop
daily.description: A shop has an “open” sign at the entrance.
daily.example: That shop is still open.

work.title: Taking a call for a colleague
work.description: Telling a client that the colleague is in a meeting.
work.example: I'm afraid Tanaka is in a meeting at the moment.

work.title: Setting a deadline
work.description: Promising to finish something within a period.
work.example: I will send you the quote by the end of tomorrow.

etymology: 「中」 is a Sino-Japanese word. 「ちゅう」 is the on-reading and keeps the Chinese sense “inside, in the middle of”. 「じゅう」 is a voiced version of the reading, and in Japanese it developed the special sense “covering the whole range”.

similar.title: 〜中 (N5)
similar.explanation: At N5 you learn only basic words like 「一日中」 and 「世界中」. At N3 you need to tell 「ちゅう」 from 「じゅう」 and learn the “in progress” and “by the deadline” uses.

similar.title: 〜最中に
similar.explanation: 「〜最中に」 stresses “right in the middle of, at the busiest moment”, often with “and then something unexpected happened”. 「〜中」 just states objectively that something is in progress.

similar.title: 〜間に
similar.explanation: 「〜間に」 can follow verbs and adjectives and means “during a period”. 「〜中」 follows only nouns and is shorter and more formal.

meaning: Means “...-style, in the style of” or “looks like a ...”. 「こんなふうに」 means “in this way”.
connection: Noun + 風 (の / に / だ); こんな etc. / 〜という + ふう (に)

senses.label: ...-style
senses.meaning: Shows the style of a region, era, or type of thing: “Japanese-style, European-style”. Common with food, architecture, and design.
senses.connection: Noun + 風の + noun / 風に (和風, 洋風, 中華風, イタリア風)
examples: Japanese-style dishes are popular at this restaurant.
I want to decorate my room in a European style.
We went into a retro Showa-era style café.

senses.label: Looks like a ...
senses.meaning: Shows that, from appearance, someone looks like a certain type of person: “office-worker-looking”. Often used to describe strangers. Objective, sometimes a guess.
senses.connection: Noun for a type of person + 風の + 人 (学生風, サラリーマン風)
examples: A man who looked like an office worker was on the phone at the station.
A young man who looked like a student asked me for directions.

senses.label: Way, manner
senses.meaning: 「こんなふうに / そんなふうに / 〜というふうに」 show the way something is done or how things are: “like this, like that”. Very common in speech.
senses.connection: こんな / そんな / あんな / どんな / こういう / 〜という + ふう (風) に / ふうな / ふうだ
examples: If you fold it like this, it comes out nicely.
I don't know how I should explain it.
I set a goal of, say, walking one hour every day.

notes: 「〜風」 is read 「ふう」, unlike 「風（かぜ）」 “wind”. In 「台風」 and 「強風」 it means wind, so they are not this pattern.
In 「こんなふうに」, 「ふう」 is usually written in kana, but 「こんな風に」 is also fine.
「〜風」 is fairly neutral when describing people, but saying it to someone's face can sound rude.

daily.title: Ordering food
daily.description: Looking at a menu and talking about the style of a dish.
daily.example: This pasta has a Japanese-style seasoning.

daily.title: Showing a friend how
daily.description: Demonstrating so the other person can copy you.
daily.example: If you hold it like this, it's not heavy.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describes a stranger's appearance.
daily.example: A man who looked like an office worker was watching us.

work.title: Discussing a design
work.description: Asking for a certain style in a design meeting.
work.example: Let's give the brochure a Scandinavian-style design.

work.title: Explaining how to work
work.description: Showing a new colleague how things are done.
work.example: Please put your reports together like this.

etymology: 「風」 originally means “wind”. In Chinese it extended to “custom, style, manner” (as in 風俗 and 作風). Japanese kept this sense and used the on-reading 「ふう」 as a suffix for “style, look”, which later developed into phrases like 「こんなふう」 for “manner”.

similar.title: 〜っぽい
similar.explanation: 「〜っぽい」 means “-ish, sort of like” and often carries a negative or subjective judgment (「子供っぽい」). 「〜風」 describes a style or look fairly objectively, without praise or criticism.

similar.title: 〜ような
similar.explanation: 「〜ような」 is used for comparisons and metaphors (「まるで夢のような話」). 「〜風」 means something really has that style (「和風の部屋」); it is not a metaphor.

similar.title: 〜型
similar.explanation: 「〜型」 means “type, model” (「最新型」, 「血液型」) and focuses on classification. 「〜風」 focuses on style and atmosphere.

meaning: After a time word, it means “for the first time in ...”. After a noun or verb masu-stem, it means “the way someone does ...”.
connection: Time word + ぶり (に / の); noun / verb masu-stem + ぶり

senses.label: For the first time in ...
senses.meaning: Shows that something happens again after a gap of time: “for the first time in (time)”. It often carries the feeling “it's been so long”.
senses.connection: Word for a length of time + ぶりに + verb / ぶりの + noun (5年ぶり, 3か月ぶり, 久しぶり)
examples: I went back to my hometown for the first time in ten years.
The first rain in three days brought the fields back to life.
Long time no see! How have you been?

senses.label: The way of doing
senses.meaning: Shows how someone does something or how they live: “the way of ...”. Often used to evaluate someone's work or lifestyle.
senses.connection: Action noun / verb masu-stem + ぶり (仕事ぶり, 話しぶり, 暮らしぶり, 生活ぶり)
examples: His serious way of working was highly praised.
Judging from the way he talks, he seems to know something.
I write about my life abroad on my blog.

senses.label: Casual: the gusto
senses.meaning: 「〜っぷり」 is the casual form, mostly in 「食べっぷり」 and 「飲みっぷり」, describing someone eating or drinking with great gusto. It carries admiration or surprise.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + っぷり (食べっぷり, 飲みっぷり)
examples: You really eat with gusto. It's a pleasure to watch.

notes: In the “first time in ...” sense, 「〜ぶり」 is used for fairly long gaps. Short ones like 「1時間ぶり」 are possible, but only if it feels like “a long time”.
「〜ぶりに」 is followed by a verb; 「〜ぶりの」 is followed by a noun.
It can be written in kanji as 「振り」, as in 「久し振り」, but kana is more common.

daily.title: Meeting an old friend
daily.description: Greeting a friend you haven't seen for years.
daily.example: It's really been ages! Five years, maybe?

daily.title: Praising a good appetite
daily.description: Seeing someone eat heartily when you treat them.
daily.example: I was amazed at how my son tucked into his food.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: Sports news reports a long-awaited win.
daily.example: The team won the championship for the first time in 15 years.

work.title: Year-end review
work.description: A boss evaluates a subordinate's performance.
work.example: Everyone recognizes Tanaka's work.

work.title: Economic news
work.description: A report says an indicator hit a record not seen for years.
work.example: The yen fell to its lowest level in about 30 years.

etymology: 「ぶり」 comes from 「振り」, the masu-stem of the verb 「振る（ふる）」, which originally meant “to wave; behavior, appearance”. After a noun it became voiced as 「ぶり」 and means “the way of ...”. After a time word it extended to “the state after that much time has passed”, giving “for the first time in ...”.

similar.title: 〜おきに
similar.explanation: 「〜おきに」 means “every other ..., at intervals of ...” and describes regular repetition. 「〜ぶりに」 only says how long since the last time, with a feeling of “at long last”.

similar.title: 〜方（かた）
similar.explanation: 「〜方」 means the method or way of doing something (「話し方」 = way of speaking) and is neutral. 「〜ぶり」 means the manner actually shown, often with evaluation (「話しぶり」 = how someone came across when talking).

similar.title: 〜よう (manner)
similar.explanation: 「〜よう」 shows a manner or degree, often exaggerated (「喜びよう」, 「慌てよう」). 「〜ぶり」 is more common for evaluating everyday performance, like work or lifestyle.

meaning: Means “each, every”: each unit is handled separately, something repeats at regular intervals, or something changes each time it happens.
connection: Noun / number word / verb dictionary form + ごとに (can be written 「毎に」)

senses.label: Each ... separately
senses.meaning: Shows that something is handled separately, or is different, for each unit: “by ..., for each ...”. Common phrases are 「〜ごとに違う」 and 「〜ごとに分ける」.
senses.connection: Noun + ごとに / ごとの + noun (国ごとに, クラスごとに, 人ごとの)
examples: Please sort your garbage by type before putting it out.
Culture and customs differ from country to country.
We will announce the results for each team.

senses.label: Every (interval)
senses.meaning: After a number word, it shows something repeating at regular intervals: “every ...”.
senses.connection: Number word + ごとに (3時間ごとに, 10分ごとに, 1年ごとに)
examples: Please take this medicine every six hours.
The bus leaves every 15 minutes.

senses.label: Each time ...
senses.meaning: After a verb, it shows that things change each time the action happens: “every time ..., more and more”. The second part usually describes a gradual change.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ごとに (会うごとに, 回を重ねるごとに)
examples: She gets prettier every time I see her.
The number of participants grows each time we hold it.

notes: 「1日ごとに」 and 「1日おきに」 are different: 「ごとに」 is every day; 「おきに」 is every other day.
「〜ごと」 on its own can also mean “including, together with”, as in 「りんごを皮ごと食べる」 (eat an apple skin and all). That is not this pattern.
With verbs, the second part is usually a gradual change, not a one-time event.

daily.title: Taking out the garbage
daily.description: A neighbor reminds a newcomer to sort the garbage.
daily.example: Each day of the week has its own type of garbage.

daily.title: Taking medicine
daily.description: A doctor explains how often to check.
daily.example: Please take your temperature every four hours.

work.title: Compiling data
work.description: Summarizing data by area.
work.example: Please summarize the sales by region.

work.title: Explaining update frequency
work.description: Telling a client how often the system updates.
work.example: The data is updated automatically every hour.

etymology: 「ごと」 is written 「毎」 in kanji and already meant “each, every” in Classical Japanese. 「ごとに」 means “by each one”. Today it is mostly written in kana, though 「毎に」 is fine in writing.

similar.title: 〜たびに
similar.explanation: 「〜たびに」 follows only verbs or “noun + の” and means “whenever ..., (always) ...”. 「〜ごとに」 can also follow number words for intervals, and with verbs it usually describes gradual change.

similar.title: 〜おきに
similar.explanation: 「〜おきに」 means “leaving a gap of ...”: 「1日おき」 is every other day, while 「1日ごと」 is every day. With longer distances or times, the two can mean almost the same.

similar.title: 〜当たり
similar.explanation: 「〜当たり」 means “per ..., on average” (「1人当たり3個」, three per person) and is used for ratios. 「〜ごとに」 means one by one, unit by unit.

meaning: Means “whenever ..., every time ...”, stressing that the same thing happens each time.
connection: Verb dictionary form / noun + の + たびに (can be written 「度に」)

senses.label: Every time ...
senses.meaning: Shows that each time you do something or meet a situation, the same result always follows: “whenever ..., every time ...”. The second part is usually something that happens naturally or a feeling.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + たびに (見るたびに, 会うたびに, 行くたびに)
examples: Every time I look at this photo, I remember my childhood.
Every time I see him, he's complaining about something.
Every time I go back home, my mom cooks a lot of food for me.

senses.label: On every (occasion)
senses.meaning: After a noun for an event or activity, it means “on every ...”. 「そのたびに」 is also common, referring back to what was said before.
senses.connection: Noun + の + たびに (試合のたびに, 旅行のたびに); そのたびに
examples: Every time I have an exam, I get so nervous my stomach hurts.
I failed many times, but each time I got back up.

notes: The second part cannot express your will or a request. ✕「会うたびに一緒に食事しよう」.
「この度（このたび）」 is a formal way to say “this time”. It is not this pattern.
You can drop 「に」 and write 「〜たび、〜」. This sounds more formal.

daily.title: Talking about memories
daily.description: A certain song brings back the past.
daily.example: Every time I hear this song, I remember my high school days.

daily.title: Complaining about family
daily.description: Telling a friend your parents always nag you.
daily.example: Every time I go home, they tell me to hurry up and get married.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describes a character's recurring feeling.
daily.example: Every time I saw his face, my heart ached.

work.title: Reviewing work problems
work.description: Pointing out in a meeting that the same problem keeps happening.
work.example: Every time we update the system, bugs appear.

work.title: Talking about business trips
work.description: Sharing your experience with colleagues.
work.example: I discover something new on every business trip.

etymology: 「たび」 is written 「度」 and is a native Japanese word that originally meant “time, occasion”. 「〜たびに」 means “on each occasion”. It sounds the same as 「旅（たび）」 “journey”, but the origins are different.

similar.title: 〜ごとに
similar.explanation: 「〜ごとに」 can follow number words for intervals, and with verbs the second part is usually a gradual change (「会うごとにきれいになる」). 「〜たびに」 stresses the same thing repeating every time.

similar.title: 〜と (condition)
similar.explanation: 「〜と」 shows a natural or habitual condition (「春になると花が咲く」), more like a general rule. 「〜たびに」 highlights “each and every time” and often includes the speaker's feelings.

similar.title: 〜とき
similar.explanation: 「〜とき」 just means “when ...” and can refer to a single time. 「〜たびに」 must be about something that happens repeatedly.

meaning: Shows that just as one action was completed, something unexpected happened right away: “the moment ..., as soon as ...”.
connection: Verb ta-form + とたん (に) (kanji: 「途端」)

senses.label: The moment ...
senses.meaning: Shows that the second event happened right after the first. The second part is usually something unexpected that the speaker couldn't control. It carries a sense of suddenness and surprise.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + とたん (に) (立ち上がったとたん, ドアを開けたとたん)
examples: The moment I stood up, I felt dizzy.
As soon as I opened the door, the cat came rushing out.
Just as I got home, it started to rain.

senses.label: Changed as soon as ...
senses.meaning: Also used to say that as soon as something happened, a person's attitude or situation changed a lot. Often critical or sarcastic.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + とたん (に) (結婚したとたん, 偉くなったとたん)
examples: As soon as he became president, he got arrogant.
The moment I brought up money, the other person's expression changed.

notes: The second part cannot be the speaker's deliberate action, a request, or an order. ✕「家に着いたとたん、電話してください」.
The second part is usually in the past tense, describing something that already happened.
「その途端」 can stand alone as a conjunction meaning “at that very moment”.

daily.title: Telling about bad luck
daily.description: Telling a friend what happened as soon as you left home.
daily.example: The moment I left the house, it started raining.

daily.title: Talking about a baby
daily.description: A mom says the baby cries as soon as she puts him down.
daily.example: As soon as I put the baby on the bed, he started crying.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describes a sudden twist.
daily.example: The moment I turned off the light, I heard someone's footsteps.

work.title: Reporting a system problem
work.description: Explaining to your boss how the problem happened.
work.example: As soon as I installed the new software, my computer stopped working.

work.title: News report
work.description: Reporting how the stock market reacted to news.
work.example: The moment the announcement was made, the stock price plunged.

etymology: 「とたん」 is written 「途端」 in kanji and means “that very moment”. 「途端」 is generally thought to be a later ateji (kanji chosen for sound), and the word's origin is debated.

similar.title: 〜か〜ないかのうちに
similar.explanation: 「〜か〜ないかのうちに」 stresses that the second event started before the first was even finished, almost at the same time. 「〜たとたん」 stresses that the first had just finished and the second happened unexpectedly.

similar.title: 〜次第
similar.explanation: 「〜次第」 means “as soon as ..., (I will do)”, and the second part is a deliberate action (「分かり次第連絡します」). After 「〜たとたん」, the second part is unexpected and not deliberate.

similar.title: 〜と同時に
similar.explanation: 「〜と同時に」 objectively says two things happened at the same time, with no surprise. 「〜たとたん」 carries a sense of suddenness and surprise.

meaning: Shows that you are right in the middle of doing something, at its peak, and often that something unexpected happened just then.
connection: Noun + の / verb te-form + いる + 最中 (に / だ)

senses.label: Right in the middle of
senses.meaning: Shows that while an action was in progress and you were busy, something else suddenly happened: “right in the middle of ...”. The second part is usually an interruption or a surprise.
senses.connection: Noun + の 最中に / verb te-form + いる + 最中に (会議の最中に, 食べている最中に)
examples: In the middle of the meeting, a cell phone rang.
The power went out while I was in the middle of a shower.
It started raining in the middle of the game.

senses.label: In the middle of (now)
senses.meaning: As a predicate, 「〜最中だ」 means you are right in the middle of something now. Often used to say you're busy.
senses.connection: Noun + の / verb te-form + いる + 最中だ / 最中です
examples: We're in the middle of discussing that issue right now.
I'm right in the thick of getting ready to move.

notes: 「真っ最中（まっさいちゅう）」 is the emphatic form: “right at the height of it”.
Read 「もなか」, 「最中」 is a kind of Japanese sweet. It has nothing to do with this pattern.
It is not used for static states that last a long time. ✕「住んでいる最中」.

daily.title: Complaining about interruptions
daily.description: Grumbling to family about a sales call during dinner.
daily.example: Right in the middle of dinner, I got a sales call.

daily.title: Turning down an invitation
daily.description: A friend invites you, but you're busy with something else.
daily.example: Sorry, I'm in the middle of writing a report right now.

work.title: Updating on progress
work.description: Answering a client's inquiry and saying it's being handled.
work.example: We are currently in the process of investigating the cause.

work.title: A meeting interrupted
work.description: Explaining afterwards how a meeting was interrupted.
work.example: The projector broke down in the middle of my presentation.

etymology: 「最中」 comes from Chinese: 「最」 is “most” and 「中」 is “middle”, together meaning “the very middle, the peak moment”. Japanese uses the on-reading 「さいちゅう」 for the most intense stage of an ongoing activity.

similar.title: 〜中（ちゅう）
similar.explanation: 「〜中」 just states objectively “in the middle of” (「会議中です」). 「〜最中に」 stresses “at the peak, at the busiest moment”, and is usually followed by a sudden event.

similar.title: 〜間に
similar.explanation: 「〜間に」 means something happened at some point during a period, long or short. 「〜最中に」 is only for the moment an action is in full swing, with a stronger sense of interruption.

similar.title: 〜ところに
similar.explanation: 「〜ところに」 means “just at that moment”, often followed by someone arriving or calling. 「〜最中に」 stresses more that the action was in full progress.

meaning: Means “when ..., on the occasion of ...”. It is a formal, written version of 「〜とき」.
connection: Noun + の / verb dictionary form or ta-form + 際 (に / は)

senses.label: When ...
senses.meaning: Shows the time when you do something or when something happens: “when ..., upon ...”. More formal than 「〜とき」 and common in notices, manuals, and business.
senses.connection: Noun + の 際 (に) / verb dictionary form or ta-form + 際 (に) (お帰りの際, 利用する際, 来た際)
examples: When leaving, please make sure you have all your belongings.
You need a photo when you apply for a passport.
When I came to Japan, I exchanged money at the airport.

senses.label: In case of ...
senses.meaning: 「〜際は」 means “in the event of ...” and explains what to do in a special situation. Common on notices and in rules.
senses.connection: Noun + の / verb dictionary form + 際は (緊急の際は, 変更する際は); その際は
examples: In an emergency, please call this number.
If you change your address, please be sure to let us know.

notes: 「〜際」 is more formal than 「〜とき」 and is rarely used in casual chat.
It is not usually used for natural phenomena or states tied to the passing of time. ✕「若い際」, ○「若いとき」.
「この際」 is a set phrase meaning “taking this opportunity”, as in 「この際、はっきり言おう」.
「〜に際して」 (N2) is even more formal and is used mostly “on the occasion of starting something important”.

daily.title: Reading a notice
daily.description: A sign in a shop or station reminds passengers.
daily.example: Please watch your step when getting off.

daily.title: Making plans with a friend
daily.description: A friend says to meet up next time, slightly formally.
daily.example: Next time you come to Tokyo, be sure to get in touch.

work.title: Writing a business email
work.description: Explaining what to do when visiting the office.
work.example: When you visit our office, please give your name at the reception desk.

work.title: Product manual
work.description: A manual lists precautions for use.
work.example: When using this product, please be sure to read the manual.

work.title: Meeting arrangements
work.description: Explaining what to do in a certain case.
work.example: If you will be absent, please let us know by the day before.

etymology: 「際」 originally means “edge, border” (as in 「水際」, the water's edge). The idea of a border in space extended to a turning point in time, so it came to mean “at the time of ...”.

similar.title: 〜とき
similar.explanation: 「〜とき」 is the most common way to say “when” and works in any situation. 「〜際」 is formal and written, used in notices and business.

similar.title: 〜に際して
similar.explanation: 「〜に際して」 is even more formal, used mostly before starting something important (「入学に際して」). 「〜際に」 has a wider range of use.

similar.title: 〜場合は
similar.explanation: 「〜場合は」 is a hypothetical “if, in case”. 「〜際は」 refers to the actual time you do something.

meaning: Shows that something happens on the way somewhere, or partway through doing something.
connection: Noun + の / verb dictionary form or te-form + いる + 途中で (に)

senses.label: On the way
senses.meaning: Shows being on the way to a place: “on the way to ...”. 「途中で」 is followed by an action; 「途中に」 is followed by existence (ある, いる).
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form (行く, 帰る, 来る) + 途中で / 途中に; noun + の 途中 (帰りの途中)
examples: I ran into a friend on my way to work.
There's a convenience store on the way home from the station.
I got caught in the rain on my way home.

senses.label: Partway through
senses.meaning: Shows that something isn't finished yet and is halfway done: “in the middle of, partway through”. The second part is often stopping, giving up, or an interruption.
senses.connection: Noun + の 途中で (話の途中, 食事の途中); verb te-form + いる + 途中で
examples: The call got cut off in the middle of our conversation.
I fell asleep halfway through the movie.
I quit the marathon partway through.

notes: 「途中で」 is followed by actions and events; 「途中に」 is followed by existence verbs like 「ある / いる」.
「途中まで」 means “up to partway”, as in 「途中まで一緒に帰ろう」.
「途中で」 on its own means “halfway”, as in 「途中で諦める」 (to give up halfway).

daily.title: Asking a family member to pick something up
daily.description: Asking someone to buy something on their way home from work.
daily.example: Could you buy some milk on your way home?

daily.title: Walking home with a friend
daily.description: After school, suggesting you walk part of the way together.
daily.example: Let's walk home together part of the way.

daily.title: Complaining about a movie
daily.description: Talking with a friend about a boring movie.
daily.example: It was so boring that I walked out halfway through.

work.title: Calling in late
work.description: Calling the office after a problem on your commute.
work.example: My train stopped on my way to work, so I'll be late.

work.title: Meeting etiquette
work.description: Reminding a new employee not to interrupt others.
work.example: Don't cut in while someone else is still talking.

etymology: 「途中」 comes from Chinese: 「途」 is “road” and 「中」 is “middle”, so it originally meant “in the middle of the road”. It later extended to “partway through a task”.

similar.title: 〜最中に
similar.explanation: 「〜最中に」 stresses that an action is at its peak, at the busiest moment. 「〜途中で」 stresses “not finished yet, halfway”, and often goes with stopping or giving up.

similar.title: 〜間に
similar.explanation: 「〜間に」 means “within a period of time”. 「〜途中で」 focuses on the point between start and finish, and can also be a physical route.

similar.title: 〜かける
similar.explanation: 「〜かける」 means an action has just started or is half done (「読みかけの本」, a half-read book). 「〜途中で」 focuses on something happening partway through.

meaning: 「〜間」 means something continues throughout a whole period; 「〜間に」 means something happens at one point within that period.
connection: Noun + の / verb dictionary form, te-form + いる, nai-form / adjective + 間 (に)

senses.label: Throughout the period
senses.meaning: 「〜間」 means that during a period, the action or state in the second part continues the whole time: “all through ..., while ...”. Often used with 「ずっと」 or 「〜ている」.
senses.connection: Noun + の / verb te-form + いる, dictionary form + 間 (は) (夏休みの間, 待っている間)
examples: I stayed at my grandmother's house the whole summer vacation.
While my mother was shopping, I waited in the car.
While I'm in Japan, I want to speak Japanese every day.

senses.label: At some point during
senses.meaning: 「〜間に」 means a one-time event happens at some point within the period: “while ..., during ...”. The second part is a one-time action.
senses.connection: Noun + の / verb te-form + いる, nai-form + 間に (留守の間に, 寝ている間に, 知らない間に)
examples: A burglar broke in while we were away.
Let's do the laundry while the kids are asleep.
Before I knew it, my hair had grown a lot.

senses.label: Between
senses.meaning: Shows space, time, or relationships between things or people: “between ..., among ...”. 「AとBの間」 is common.
senses.connection: Noun A + と + noun B + の + 間 (に)
examples: There's a bank between the station and the post office.
This app is popular among young people.

notes: Key point: 「間」 is followed by a continuing action (ずっと〜ていた); 「間に」 by a one-time action (〜した).
「この間」 read 「このあいだ」 means “the other day” and is not this pattern. 「いつの間にか」 is a set phrase meaning “before I knew it”.
「間に合う」 is read 「まにあう」 and means “to be in time”. It has nothing to do with this pattern.

daily.title: Asking family for a favor
daily.description: Before going out, asking someone to accept a delivery.
daily.example: If a package comes while I'm out, could you take it for me?

daily.title: Talking about studying abroad
daily.description: Telling a friend about life while studying abroad.
daily.example: I lived in a dorm the whole time I was studying abroad.

daily.title: Watching a child grow
daily.description: Being amazed at how fast a child grows.
daily.example: You've grown so much since I last saw you!

work.title: Assigning tasks
work.description: A boss asks you to prepare materials during a meeting.
work.example: While the meeting is going on, please make copies of the materials.

work.title: Handing over work
work.description: Asking a colleague to take over during a business trip.
work.example: While I'm on my business trip, I'll leave this matter to Yamada.

etymology: 「間（あいだ）」 is a native Japanese word that originally meant “the gap between two things”. The sense of space “between” extended to time, “a period”. One theory links it to 「合う（あう）」, but this is not settled.

similar.title: 〜間・〜間に (N4)
similar.explanation: You learned the basics at N4. At N3 the focus is telling 「間」 (continuous over the whole period) from 「間に」 (a one-time action within it), and set phrases like 「知らない間に」.

similar.title: 〜うちに
similar.explanation: 「〜うちに」 stresses “while the state lasts, before it changes” (「若いうちに」, 「熱いうちに」), or a change happening unnoticed. 「〜間に」 objectively marks a period with a clearer start and end.

similar.title: 〜最中に
similar.explanation: 「〜最中に」 is only for the busy moment when an action is in full swing, usually with an interruption. 「〜間に」 is broader and doesn't have to involve a surprise.

meaning: Shows that only after experiencing something did you realize or understand something you hadn't noticed before: “not until ...”.
connection: Verb te-form + 初めて (はじめて)

senses.label: Not until ...
senses.meaning: Shows that only after the first experience did you understand or notice the second: “it wasn't until ... that ...”. The second part is usually a verb of understanding like 「分かる」, 「気づく」 or 「知る」.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + 初めて + 分かる / 気づく / 知る (失って初めて, 親になって初めて)
examples: It wasn't until I got sick that I realized how important health is.
It wasn't until I became a parent that I realized how hard my parents had worked.
Only after living alone did I learn how hard housework is.

senses.label: Only when ... can ...
senses.meaning: Shows that the second part is only possible once the first condition is met: “only when ... can ...”. Often used as 「〜て初めて〜できる」. Somewhat formal.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + 初めて + potential form / becomes possible (話し合って初めて, 努力して初めて)
examples: Only when you actually try using it do you see how good it is.
Only by talking things through with each other can we solve the problem.

notes: The second part cannot express the speaker's will or a request. ✕「日本に来て初めて、日本語を勉強しよう」.
「生まれて初めて」 is a set phrase meaning “for the first time in my life”.
In 「日本で初めて」 and 「女性として初めて」, 「初めて」 means “the first (one)”. That is not this pattern.

daily.title: Thanking your parents
daily.description: Calling home to say thanks after moving out.
daily.example: It wasn't until I lived on my own that I realized how much Mom did for me.

daily.title: Talking about a trip
daily.description: Sharing impressions with a friend after a trip.
daily.example: It wasn't until I actually went there that I saw how great that country is.

work.title: Reflecting on work
work.description: A new employee writes what they learned in a report.
work.example: It wasn't until I actually worked on site that I realized how important customer feedback is.

work.title: Written commentary
work.description: A newspaper column stresses the importance of practice.
work.example: Only when a system is actually put into practice do its problems become clear.

etymology: 「初めて」 comes from the te-form of the old verb 「初める（はじめる）」, which turned into an adverb meaning “for the first time”. After 「〜て」, it means “only after the first thing, for the first time (did I understand)”.

similar.title: 〜てから
similar.explanation: 「〜てから」 just shows the order of events. 「〜て初めて」 stresses “not before, but only after this, for the first time”, with a sense of sudden realization.

similar.title: 〜てからでないと
similar.explanation: 「〜てからでないと」 means “you can't ... unless you first ...”, and the second part is usually negative. After 「〜て初めて」, the second part is usually a positive realization.

similar.title: 〜てからというもの
similar.explanation: 「〜てからというもの」 means “ever since ..., (things have been) ...”, stressing a lasting change afterwards. 「〜て初めて」 stresses the moment you first understood.

meaning: Means “unless you first ..., you can't ...”, stressing that the first action is a necessary condition for the second.
connection: Verb te-form + からでないと (からでなければ) + negative / difficult outcome

senses.label: Can't ... unless first ...
senses.meaning: Shows that the first thing must be done, or the second can't happen: “not until ..., unless you first ...”. The second part is usually negative or something like 「無理だ」 or 「困る」.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + からでないと / からでなければ + 〜ない・〜できない・無理だ
examples: I can't decide until I've talked it over with my parents.
You can't go in until you've paid.
I can't say anything until I've seen the actual item.

senses.label: Casual forms
senses.meaning: In speech, people often say 「〜てからじゃないと」 or 「〜てからでなきゃ」. Casual tone, same meaning.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + からじゃないと / からでなきゃ / からじゃなきゃ
examples: You can't go out and play until you've finished your homework.
If you don't prepare properly first, it won't go well.

notes: The second part is usually negative, not a positive statement of will.
「からでなければ」 is more formal than 「からでないと」.
Common when declining or postponing an answer: 「上司に確認してからでないと、お答えできません」.

daily.title: A mother's reminder
daily.description: A mother tells her child to wash hands before a snack.
daily.example: No snacks until you've washed your hands.

daily.title: Unsure while shopping
daily.description: Out shopping with a friend, wanting to try something on first.
daily.example: I can't decide whether to buy it until I try it on.

work.title: Postponing a reply to a client
work.description: A client wants an answer now; you politely say you need to check first.
work.example: I'm afraid I can't give you an answer until I've checked with my manager.

work.title: Explaining a procedure
work.description: Telling a new employee what's required before using a system.
work.example: You can't use this system until you've completed the training.

etymology: It is made from 「〜てから」 (after ...) + 「でない」 (is not) + 「と」 (if). Literally “if it is not after ...”, meaning “unless you first ...”.

similar.title: 〜て初めて
similar.explanation: 「〜て初めて」 means you understood only after an experience, and the second part is usually positive. 「〜てからでないと」 means “not possible unless you first ...”, and the second part is usually negative.

similar.title: 〜てから
similar.explanation: 「〜てから」 just shows order. 「〜てからでないと」 stresses that the first action is an essential precondition.

similar.title: 〜なければならない
similar.explanation: 「〜なければならない」 directly says “you must do ...”. 「〜てからでないと」 says “you can't ... unless you first ...”, stressing the precondition through its consequence.

meaning: After a noun, it means “only, just”. After a verb ta-form, it means “did ... and then never again”. After a verb masu-stem, it means “constantly, devoted to ...”.
connection: Noun / これ・それ・あれ + きり; verb ta-form + きり; verb masu-stem + きり (often 〜っきり in speech)

senses.label: Only, just
senses.meaning: After a number word or noun, it limits: “only, just”. Common forms are 「二人きり」, 「一度きり」 and 「これきり」. It stresses “just this, nothing more” more strongly than 「だけ」.
senses.connection: Noun / number word + きり (二人きり, 一度きり); これ・それ・あれ + きり
examples: We're finally alone together, just the two of us.
You only get one chance.
I haven't seen him since then.

senses.label: ... and never again
senses.meaning: 「〜たきり」 shows that after doing something, things stayed that way with nothing following: “did ... and then never ...”. The second part is usually negative, with a sense of surprise or worry.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + きり (〜ない) (出かけたきり, 寝たきり)
examples: My son went out this morning and still hasn't come back.
I lent her a book, and she never gave it back.
My grandfather has been bedridden since last year.

senses.label: Constantly, fully devoted
senses.meaning: After some verb masu-stems, it shows being fully focused on one thing and doing nothing else: “constantly at someone's side, tied up with”. Common in 「付ききり」 and 「かかりきり」.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + きり (付ききり, かかりきり; casual: 付きっきり)
examples: My mother stayed by my sick little brother's side all night.
I've been completely tied up with this project and have no time to rest.

notes: In speech it often becomes 「〜っきり」, as in 「一人っきり」 and 「あれっきり」.
After 「〜たきり」 the second part is usually negative, meaning “nothing has changed since then”.
The 「きり」 in adverbs like 「はっきり」 and 「すっきり」 has nothing to do with this pattern.
At N2, 「〜きり」 has more formal uses, which you can compare later.

daily.title: Worrying about family
daily.description: A family member went out and hasn't been in touch.
daily.example: My sister went out at noon and we haven't heard from her since.

daily.title: On a date
daily.description: A couple finally gets some time alone.
daily.example: Let's go out today, just the two of us, for the first time in a while.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describes characters who never met again after parting.
daily.example: After we parted that day, I never saw him again.

work.title: Chasing a reply
work.description: Complaining to a colleague that the other side hasn't replied.
work.example: I sent them an email, but I still haven't heard back.

work.title: Explaining your workload
work.description: Telling your boss you've been focused on one task.
work.example: This week I was completely tied up with preparing the new product.

etymology: 「きり」 comes from 「切り」, the masu-stem of the verb 「切る（きる）」 “to cut”. From “cut off, stop here”, it extended to “limited to this” and “cut off there, with nothing after”.

similar.title: 〜だけ
similar.explanation: 「〜だけ」 is the general “only”. 「〜きり」 stresses “just this once, nothing else” more strongly and often carries emotion (「二人きり」, 「一度きり」).

similar.title: 〜まま
similar.explanation: 「〜まま」 means a state stays unchanged (「窓を開けたまま寝た」). 「〜たきり」 stresses “did it and then nothing followed”, and the second part is usually negative.

similar.title: 〜きり (N2)
similar.explanation: N2 「〜きり」 includes more formal uses. At N3, focus on common forms like 「二人きり」, 「〜たきり〜ない」 and 「付ききり」.

similar.title: 〜切る
similar.explanation: 「〜切る」 is a compound verb meaning “do completely” (「読み切る」, 「疲れ切る」). 「〜きり」 means a limit or “nothing after that”, which is different.
